I have been working this land for fifty years. I know what the soil needs, what the weather does, and what my body can handle at seventy-five. My sons and daughters mostly work away in the city now, so I cannot count on them for the heavy seasons. My wife and one younger person in the house help me. I must plan carefully.

My fourteen mu is split between two systems. Ten mu runs the wheat-maize rotation — that is my stable income and our food. The other four mu I grow cotton. Cotton is hard work, but I have grown it my whole life and the price is still worth it for a small plot. I will not expand it because picking is too difficult with just a few hands.

**Wheat (planted October, harvested June):** I will buy improved seed from the township seed station — same variety I have used for many years, good straw strength, decent yield. I apply base fertilizer before sowing and topdress at jointing. I irrigate four times: before sowing to ensure germination, then again in winter to protect against frost heave, at jointing, and at heading. Two pesticide passes — one herbicide in winter, one for aphids and mildew in spring.

**Maize (planted June after wheat, harvested October):** I use hybrid seed, everyone does now and the yield is much better. I seed directly into the stubble without plowing — saves my back and saves time during the tight wheat-maize turnover window. I topdress nitrogen at the V6 stage and again near tasseling. Two irrigations — one at silking if rain is short, one at grain fill. Two pesticide applications for corn borer and herbicide.

**Cotton (planted April, harvested September-October):** Hybrid Bt seed, saves me from the worst of the bollworm. Plough in early spring to break up the winter soil. Cotton needs more water than maize — I irrigate four times across the season. Pesticide I apply five times, it still needs it even with Bt for aphids and spider mites. I apply heavy potassium because I have found my cotton lint quality is better for it.
